Subject: Follow-up: embeddings migration details from today's call

Thanks for the call earlier — helpful session. Two quick asks we want captured before the technical deep-dive next week: 

1) Dimension guidance: Our existing vendor (VectorCloud) uses 1536 dims. We want to understand tradeoffs for moving to 768 vs keeping 1536 (latency, recall for product search, storage cost).
2) Normalization: currently we L2-normalize vectors on ingest. Any recommendations if we migrate with pre-normalized vectors vs re-normalizing on Redwood?
3) Batching & rate limits: our ingest pipeline peaks at 120k vectors/day with bursty traffic. What's a safe batching size and concurrency strategy on Redwood Dedicated to keep latency under 50ms for embeddings queries?
4) Migration approach: exporting vectors from VectorCloud (CSV sample attached), reindex vs delta reindex, and how to handle idempotency when we do incremental resyncs.
5) SDK & auth: Our infra team prefers Go for ingesters and wants OIDC-based auth with short-lived tokens; we also need a node/python option for the inference side. Any turnkey SDK recommendations or examples?

Can you confirm if Redwood has a recommended canary plan (index subset first) and any tooling to compare similarity distributions pre/post migration? We'll attach a small csv export of 1k vectors.

Thanks — Samir
Samir Shah
Head of Search & Relevance, Nordgate Retail

Samir — great questions and thanks for the sample. High-level answers and proposed next steps below; Karthik and I can deep-dive on the tech call Monday.

Short answers:
- Dimensions: 768 is a reasonable middle-ground for cost/latency with models in our catalog (esp. open models optimized for 768). For highest recall on complicated SKU semantics, 1536 can help but comes with ~1.6–2x storage and modest latency penalties. We'll share benchmark numbers for your corpus on the call.
- Normalization: if vectors are already L2-normalized, you can keep them as-is. Re-normalizing in Redwood is cheap at ingest time but necessary if you change model or pooling. For migration we recommend re-normalizing during reindex to ensure consistency.
- Batching: start with batch sizes of 256 for CPU-side pre-processing and 64 for GPU-side embed calls; tune against latency targets. For queries, continuous batching on Redwood favors smaller per-request batch sizes with higher concurrency. We'll map your 120k/day into steady-state qps and provide a throughput plan.
- Migration: recommended cutover — (1) index a 10% canary slice, (2) run A/B similarity checks, (3) full reindex with idempotent upserts. For delta syncs, include a last_modified timestamp and tombstone flag.
- SDK/Auth: we support official Python and Node SDKs; Go is supported via our HTTP API + a small Go client we maintain. We support API keys, API key rotation, and short-lived OIDC tokens via our Private deployments (we'll share an example OIDC config).

Next steps (action items):
- Karthik: propose a dimension/quantization benchmark matrix for Nordgate (we'll attach this).
- Jonas: share a migration checklist + sample reindex script (attached).
- Marissa: align procurement timelines and Dedicated capacity estimate with Nordgate procurement.
- Samir/Elena: confirm a 60–90 minute technical deep dive Monday 4/16 or Tuesday 4/17 (your timezone).

Attachments: migration-checklist.xlsx (xlsx), auth-routing.drawio (diagram)

Thanks,
Jonas Weber

Samir — added a few technical notes for the pre-call reading: 

1) Dimensionality recommendation: 768 + fp16 quantization gives a strong latency/cost sweet spot for our recommended retriever models. If you keep 1536, consider PQ/quantization on dedicated to reduce storage; we can show tradeoffs.
2) Normalization: We'll re-normalize during reindex and store raw + normalized versions if you want to experiment. Storing both increases storage ~1.3x but gives flexibility.
3) Batch sizing: For your daily ingestion profile, we recommend an async ingest pipeline that batches at 512 on the producer side and issues concurrent (8) requests of 64 vectors to Redwood ingest API. That pattern keeps per-call latency stable and maximizes throughput.
4) Canary & validation: We'll provide a script to compute recall@k and mean cosine drift between old and new indices. Also suggest capturing distribution histograms pre/post for drift alerts.

I'll bring a short benchmark table to the call (latency vs storage vs recall) and we'll run it on your sample.

—Karthik
Principal Inference Engineer, Redwood Inference
